title: Security review: Encryption & KMS (BYOK/HSM) - Helix Insurance
next_steps: Send SOC2 report and encryption whitepaper - Aisha
Share BYOK integration guide and sample IaC - Daniel
Schedule PoC/benchmarks with Helix infra team - Aisha & Marcus
Follow up on HSM attestation questions - Daniel
action_items: Laura Chen: Provide list of regulated workloads to scope BYOK (due 2026-04-10)
Daniel Kim: Share BYOK integration doc and sample Terraform (due 2026-03-31)
Aisha Patel: Send SOC2 report and audit log retention details (due 2026-03-29)
summary: Redwood walked Helix Insurance through encryption at rest and in transit, KMS options including BYOK and HSM, differences across Hosted/Dedicated/Private deployments, and audit/logging capabilities. Customer raised questions about HSM attestation, multi-region key replication, and key rotation processes. Agreed next steps: share docs, run PoC benchmarks, and schedule follow-up tech deep-dive.
transcript:
[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you taking the time. Quick intro, I'm Aisha Patel, AE at Redwood. Daniel is our solutions engineer. Who do we have from Helix?
[00:10] Laura: Hi, Laura Chen, CISO at Helix Insurance.
[00:12] Marcus: Marcus Reyes, Head of Cloud.
[00:14] Sonia: Sonia Patel, security engineer.
[00:18] Aisha: Great, goal for today is to run through encryption at rest and in-transit, our KMS options, BYOK flow and HSM attestation, and logging. We'll leave time for questions.
[00:30] Daniel: Quick note, I'll show the high-level architecture for Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Also call out where keys live, how rotations work, and what the HSM path looks like.
[00:42] Laura: We're primarily concerned with data residency and FIP- something, I mean PCI and HIPAA scopes, and also we need FIPS 140-2 alignment for keys if possible.
[00:55] Marcus: Our current stack is AWS, we use AWS KMS with Customer Managed Keys and CloudHSM for certain services. We want to understand how Redwood plugs in and whether we can bring our own keys.
[01:08] Daniel: Totally, Redwood supports multiple modes. For our Hosted API we default to platform-managed keys. Data at rest is encrypted with AES-256, and we use TLS 1.2/1.3 for in-transit. For customers who require BYOK, we support a BYOK flow that integrates with AWS KMS and with external HSMs via PKCS#11 or CloudHSM bridging.
[01:30] Sonia: How does key ownership look? If we bring keys, do we retain control?
[01:34] Daniel: Yes — with BYOK you retain control of key material. The flow is: you create a key in your KMS (or HSM), grant Redwood a wrapping key or import a public key, we encrypt model cache and storage objects with a data key that is envelope-encrypted by your CMK. Redwood never sees your plaintext CMK.
[01:50] Marcus: And rotation? We have strict rotation policies, often 90 days for some keys.
[01:55] Daniel: We support automatic rewrapping on rotation. The data keys are re-encrypted under the new CMK version; we keep versioning to allow rollback for a short window. There's a small maintenance window for large bulk rewraps but it's designed to be transparent to inference.
[02:10] Laura: We also need HSM attestation — can you provide an attestation or integration with our CloudHSM’s attestation?
[02:16] Aisha: Daniel, do you want to take HSM attestation?
[02:18] Daniel: Sure. For CloudHSM we can integrate using the native client; for on-prem HSMs we support PKCS#11 and can work with vendors like Thales and Utimaco. We can bring the HSM endpoint into our Private deployment so the HSM is in your VPC and Redwood's control plane never has access to the key. Attestation docs and FIPS reports are in the security whitepaper; we'll share those.
[02:40] Sonia: A couple of clarifying questions — audit logging, who sees the key usage logs and how long are they retained?
[02:46] Daniel: We emit detailed audit logs for key usage and KMS operations. In Hosted mode, logs are retained per our standard retention (90 days) and can be exported to customer-owned S3 or SIEM via our integration. For Dedicated and Private, you can route logs directly to your logging stack and set retention to meet compliance. Access controls are RBAC-based; only authorized service accounts will perform key operations.
[03:10] Marcus: What about multi-region key replication? We have cross-region DR needs.
[03:15] Daniel: We support key replication patterns. With customer-managed KMS, replication is handled by your KMS (e.g., AWS KMS multi-region keys). For Redwood's managed keys, we replicate encrypted blobs across regions but recommend customer-managed multi-region keys for full compliance — we can document tradeoffs.
[03:32] Laura: Any latency impact for BYOK vs platform keys?
[03:36] Daniel: Minimal. Envelope encryption keeps per-request KMS calls rare — we cache data keys in the runtime's protected cache (we call it KV cache, sometimes transcribed as KV cash), so the per-token path is unchanged. The one-time unwrapping on rotate or at provisioning is the main KMS call.
[03:54] Sonia: How do you secure the runtime cache? If it's compromised, could keys be exfiltrated?
[03:59] Daniel: The runtime stores the keys in a sealed memory region and uses process isolation. On Dedicated/Private, you can also enable mTLS and customer-side HSM wrapping so even runtime-held keys are wrapped by a key only you hold. Plus we support hardware-backed enclaves for certain partners.
[04:16] Marcus: For Private deployment, you mentioned the control plane is optional. If we run Private, can we keep all key material in our VPC and keep Redwood boxed to the control plane only?
[04:24] Daniel: Yes. In our Private product we deploy a control plane that manages metadata, but all encryption, inference runtime, and KMS calls can be configured to be inside your VPC. We support an air-gapped mode for highly regulated customers where the control plane is customer-hosted.
[04:40] Laura: Regarding SOC2 and ISO stuff, do you have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001 certs?
[04:44] Aisha: Yes, we have SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001. We'll share the audit report under an NDA.
[04:50] Sonia: What about key compromise scenarios? If a key is compromised, what's the recommended remediation?
[04:55] Daniel: Revoke and rotate the CMK, rewrap data keys, and we have a forensic playbook. We also support 'key zeroization' for HSMs where the key is destroyed. We'll work with your security team to run tabletop scenarios.
[05:10] Marcus: Any limit on key usage rate? We have high throughput for inference, could KMS API rate limits be an issue?
[05:16] Daniel: Envelope encryption avoids per-inference KMS calls. You do get occasional calls for rewraps and cold-starts. For extreme throughput, we recommend Dedicated with local cache and optionally a local KMS proxy in your VPC to buffer KMS requests.
[05:32] Laura: Can Redwood's log exports be sent to our SIEM and include key operation entries? We need to ingest into Splunk.
[05:38] Daniel: Yes, we can push logs to customer SIEMs. For Hosted customers we provide a push-to-S3 or streaming option; Dedicated/Private can deliver directly via secure syslog or a Kinesis/Firehose integration.
[05:52] Sonia: How granular is RBAC? We need separation of duties between ops and security.
[05:56] Daniel: RBAC is role-based with fine-grained permissions — you can limit key management ops to a small set. We integrate with SSO/SAML for provisioning and support SCIM for user lifecycle.
[06:10] Aisha: I'm going to share two links in the chat: security whitepaper and the BYOK quickstart.
[06:15] Marcus: Thanks.
[06:17] Daniel: A quick architecture slide — for Hosted we keep encrypted blobs in our storage, wrapped by your CMK. For Dedicated we run inference in customer-dedicated GPU nodes; keys are still wrapped the same way. For Private we recommend local HSM and control plane connectors.
[06:35] Laura: Are there any certifications for the HSM integrations? We need FIPS validation and vendor attestation.
[06:40] Daniel: We can provide vendor attestation docs and our integration test results. For CloudHSM we rely on AWS's FIPS 140-2 validated HSM; for on-prem HSMs we request the customer's attestation and then run provable integration tests. We'll share sample attestation language.
[06:55] Sonia: About key rotation windows — if a key rotates, how long before old data becomes unreadable?
[07:01] Daniel: We keep old CMK versions available for a defined retention — usually 30 days for rollback. After that, if you schedule deletion, data rewrap is required and old ciphertext may become unreadable. We log each decryption event to audit logs.
[07:18] Marcus: For disaster recovery, do you replicate keys cross-account? We sometimes have separate AWS accounts per region.
[07:25] Daniel: For cross-account replication you can either use cross-account grants in AWS KMS or replicate wrapped blobs and have separate CMKs in each account. We'll provide patterns.
[07:36] Laura: Any impact on model performance for encryption-enabled storage?
[07:40] Daniel: Negligible at token path. Storage-level encryption/decryption is off the critical path due to caching. Model weights are loaded into runtime memory decrypted locally; that's handled during cold starts.
[07:54] Sonia: Do you support HSM-backed signing for audit logs? We want tamper-evident logs.
[07:59] Daniel: We support HMAC signing and can route log signing through a customer HSM for non-repudiation. The log stream includes immutable append-only sequences.
[08:12] Laura: Is there any scenario where Redwood holds unencrypted customer data?
[08:16] Aisha: Our policy is we do not persist PII beyond what the SLA permits; for Hosted we have retention windows. For Dedicated/Private, data resides in customer-controlled storage.
[08:28] Marcus: One more thing — can we do an end-to-end flow: key generation in our KMS, provide public key, Redwood does wrap/unwrapping and show the logs? A PoC.
[08:36] Daniel: Yes, absolutely. Typical PoC steps are: 1) define scope and datasets, 2) provision a test key, 3) run sample workload and measure KMS calls and latency, 4) validate logs and key operations.
[08:50] Sonia: Are there special considerations for embeddings or cached responses?
[08:54] Daniel: Embeddings are stored encrypted as well; caching respects data classification and you can opt out of caching for certain routes. We also support token-level redaction for PII.
[09:05] Laura: Ok, let's talk about the BYOK onboarding steps in detail.
[09:09] Daniel: Step one is signing the necessary agreements for key custody. Step two is creating a CMK in your KMS, or provisioning HSM keys. Step three is granting Redwood the necessary grant/role to encrypt the data key, or set up a wrapping key that Redwood uses to envelope. We'll provide Terraform snippets and the minimal IAM role.
[09:31] Marcus: IAM granularity — we need least privilege.
[09:34] Daniel: We'll share a minimal policy with kms:Encrypt/kms:Decrypt and KMS grants scoped to the test keys. We recommend service accounts rather than broad user credentials.
[09:45] Laura: One compliance ask — can we get proof that key material is never exfiltrated?
[09:50] Aisha: We can provide an attestation and the SOC2 report. For additional assurance, Private deployment with on-prem HSM is the strongest option.
[09:59] Sonia: On logging, can we get per-key rotation logs and a timeline?
[10:03] Daniel: Yes, rotation events, grant changes and decrypt calls are all logged with resource identifiers. We'll produce an example log extract.
[10:13] Marcus: Are there any known caveats integrating with non-AWS KMS?
[10:18] Daniel: We support GCP KMS and Azure Key Vault via their respective APIs; on-prem HSMs are more bespoke and require some integration testing. Occasionally we see latency differences or auth model differences, but those are solvable.
[10:33] Laura: For the HSM attestation, what level of detail is in the document? Is it the vendor's cert or Redwood's own test results?
[10:40] Daniel: Both — vendor certs plus our integration test summary and logs. If you need deeper evidence, we can negotiate a joint attestation exercise.
[10:52] Sonia: A question about key deletion — if a key is scheduled for deletion, what happens to live inference jobs?
[10:57] Daniel: If deletion is scheduled, we recommend a careful rollback window. Live jobs that need the key must complete or we rewrap before deletion. The system prevents accidental deletion without an approved process.
[11:12] Marcus: Let's cover the network encryption — you said TLS 1.2/1.3, any mutual TLS?
[11:17] Daniel: We support mTLS for Dedicated and Private deployments; for Hosted we support TLS with strict cipher suites and optional client certs. You can enable mTLS to the inference endpoints for additional protection.
[11:32] Laura: Will you share the sample IAM policies and terraform?
[11:35] Aisha: Yes, we'll put them in the follow-up package.
[11:37] (sound of typing)
[11:40] Daniel: I'm going to mark an internal note — for Helix, recommended path is Private or Dedicated plus BYOK.
[11:46] Sonia: Timeline: we have an internal quarter-end in mid-April, so we'd like pilot by early April.
[11:52] Aisha: We'll aim to support that.
[11:54] Daniel: On the PoC, we can scope a small ML workload and run perf benchmarks — we'll capture KMS call rates and latency.
[12:03] Laura: Any additional security controls for the runtime? Secrets rotation?
[12:08] Daniel: Yes, we rotate service credentials, and for long-lived secrets we recommend using the HSM-backed keys. We provide key rotation automation hooks.
[12:20] Marcus: Any audit log retention options longer than 90 days? For legal we sometimes need seven years.
[12:25] Daniel: For Hosted we can do extended retention as an add-on. For Dedicated/Private you control retention. We'll include pricing options.
[12:36] Sonia: Regarding SAML provisioning, does Redwood support our IdP and SCIM?
[12:40] Daniel: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM user provisioning are supported.
[12:45] Aisha: Ok folks, we're at about ~12 minutes in on my timer; I know the call is scheduled for 15 minutes so we'll wrap soon. Any burning questions?
[12:55] Laura: Could you clarify the 'sealed memory' comment — is it an enclave?
[13:00] Daniel: For certain partners we use SGX-style enclaves; generally it's OS-level sealed memory and kernel protections. We can discuss enclave options in the follow-up deep-dive.
[13:16] Sonia: Can we get example logs that show KMS grants and decryption events?
[13:20] Daniel: Yes, example logs will be in the share.
[13:25] Marcus: For private HSMs, we'll need to coordinate network connectivity — firewall rules, peering, etc.
[13:31] Aisha: We'll include a network checklist in the PoC doc.
[13:35] Laura: What's the escalation path if we see suspicious key usage?
[13:39] Daniel: Our security response team pairs with customer sec teams. We have on-call for incidents and define SLAs in the enterprise agreement.
[13:49] Sonia: Any suggestions for limiting blast radius for embeddings?
[13:53] Daniel: You can disable caching on routes with embeddings or enable per-route encryption keys. Also we support classification tags and token redaction.
[14:05] Marcus: Ok, let's talk about testing schedule — can you do a two-week PoC with a test key?
[14:10] Daniel: Yes, two-week PoC is feasible. We'll need access to a test KMS and a small sample dataset.
[14:20] Laura: For legal, we'll need an NDA to share certain attestation docs.
[14:24] Aisha: Noted — we'll route the SOC2 under NDA.
[14:28] (brief pause)
[14:33] Aisha: Any other items? If not, let's recap next steps.
[14:38] Daniel: Recap: Share BYOK quickstart, sample IAM policies, SOC2 report and attestation docs, schedule PoC and follow-up deep dive on HSM attestation and enclave options.
[14:51] Aisha: Action items noted — I'll send calendar invites and the docs.
[14:55] Laura: Thanks all.
[14:57] Marcus: Thank you.
[15:00] Sonia: Appreciate it.
[15:02] Aisha: Thanks everyone, bye.
